Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply 10 questions about your mood, anxiety, and thoughts over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team unless safety is a concern. We’ll go one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words. Ready to start?

First question: Over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly, most of the time it feels pretty difficult. My sister sent me a funny video the other day and I just… couldn’t really laugh. I smiled a little, but it felt forced. Things that used to crack me up before the baby now just feel flat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I mean, I can force a small smile sometimes, but actually laughing—like really laughing—hasn’t happened much at all this week.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I used to be excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower. This week, nothing really feels worth looking forward to. I still go through the motions, but the spark isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong or I’m not good enough as a mom. Even little stuff like spilling a bottle—my head jumps straight to “I’m failing.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there with the baby asleep and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure something awful is about to happen—like I’ll trip on the stairs or the milk isn’t good enough. There’s no real reason, but the thoughts just keep looping.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week I’ve gotten that sudden wave—like my chest tightens and I can’t catch my breath. It hits out of nowhere, even when the baby’s fine and the room is quiet. I tell myself there’s nothing to fear, but my body doesn’t listen.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. Dishes pile up, the baby needs feeding, laundry’s everywhere, and I just freeze, thinking, “I can’t do all this.” I still manage, but it’s like walking through thick mud.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t shut off. I keep replaying everything I might’ve messed up that day, worrying about the baby breathing, worrying I’m a bad mom. It takes me over an hour to fall asleep, and then I wake up two or three times with my heart pounding.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. I wake up with this heavy, grey feeling that just sits on me. I can still get up and do what the baby needs, but I’m going through the motions—inside I just feel flat and weepy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Twice this week I just broke down—once when the baby wouldn’t latch and once after a phone call with my mom. The tears came out of nowhere and I couldn’t stop them. It felt like all the pressure just spilled over.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yeah… a couple of times, when everything felt too heavy, the idea kind of flickered through my mind—like “what if I just wasn’t here?” It scared me; I don’t have a plan or any real wish to do it, but the thought did show up.

documents.highlight: A serial cross-sectional analysis of nearly 8 million (n 57,906,820) delivery hospitalizations identified in the National Inpa- tient Sample, representing almost 40 million (n539,024,974) deliveries in the United States occurring from 2006 to 2015, found that perinatal mood and anxietydisorders increased from 18.4 per 1,000 deliveries (95% CI 16.4 –20.0) to 40.4 per 1,000 deliveries (95% CI 39.3 – 41.6) and that severe mental illness increased from 4.2 per 1,000 deliveries (95% CI 3.9 –4.6) to 8.1 per 1,000 deliveries (95% CI 7.9 –8.4) (5).

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Summary  

**Presenting symptoms:**  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness  
- Marked guilt / self-blame (“failing as a mom”)  
- Recurrent, intrusive worry and panic symptoms (daily, unprompted)  
- Overwhelm and “freeze” response to routine tasks  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance difficulties driven by rumination  
- Passive suicidal ideation (no plan or intent)  

**Pattern:**  
Symptoms present most days this past week; interfere with functioning and attachment experiences.  

**Screening significance:**  
- High endorsement consistent with probable major depressive episode with anxious features, peripartum onset  
- Passive self-harm thoughts elevate safety risk  

**Immediate considerations:**  
1. Safety assessment (frequency/intensity of suicidal thoughts, protective factors, supports)  
2. Further evaluation for postpartum depression and anxiety (diagnostic interview, standardized scales)  
3. Psycho-education and referral options discussed / offered
